questions.question: What are the states a Java thread can be in, and how does it move between them?
questions.title: Java Thread Lifecycle (States)
questions.direct_answer: A Java thread is in one of six states defined by Thread.State: NEW (created but not started), RUNNABLE (started and ready/running, waiting for CPU or I/O), BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor lock to enter a synchronized region), WAITING (waiting indefinitely after wait()/join()/LockSupport.park()), TIMED_WAITING (waiting for a bounded time after sleep(ms)/wait(ms)/join(ms)), and TERMINATED (run() finished). It moves between them via start() (NEW→RUNNABLE), synchronized contention (RUNNABLE→BLOCKED), wait()/sleep()/join() (→WAITING/TIMED_WAITING), notify()/timeout/return (→RUNNABLE), and run() returning (→TERMINATED).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the six states and the transitions: NEW→RUNNABLE (start), RUNNABLE↔BLOCKED (lock), →WAITING/TIMED_WAITING (wait/sleep), →TERMINATED.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing BLOCKED (waiting for a lock) with WAITING (waiting for notify), or thinking RUNNABLE means 'currently running' (it means ready/running/I/O).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Six states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED. Know the transitions: start, lock contention, wait/sleep, notify, run() returning.

sections.title: Six States and Their Transitions
sections.content: A Java thread is always in exactly one of six states defined by Thread.State. NEW: created but start() not called. RUNNABLE: start() was called; the thread is ready, running, or doing I/O (the JVM combines 'ready' and 'running' under one label). BLOCKED: waiting to acquire a monitor lock to enter a synchronized region. WAITING: waiting indefinitely after calling wait(), join(), or park() without a timeout. TIMED_WAITING: waiting for a bounded time after sleep(ms), wait(ms), or join(ms). TERMINATED: run() has finished (normally or by exception). The transitions: start() moves NEW→RUNNABLE; synchronized contention moves RUNNABLE→BLOCKED (back to RUNNABLE when the lock is acquired); wait()/sleep()/join() move to WAITING/TIMED_WAITING and notify()/timeout return to RUNNABLE; run() returning moves to TERMINATED.

sections.title: The Thread State Machine
sections.content:
A thread moves through six states based on start, lock contention, wait/sleep, and run() returning.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> NEW
  NEW --> RUNNABLE: start()
  RUNNABLE --> BLOCKED: synchronized (lock held)
  BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE: lock acquired
  RUNNABLE --> WAITING: wait()/join()
  RUNNABLE --> TIMED_WAITING: sleep(ms)/wait(ms)
  WAITING --> RUNNABLE: notify()
  TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE: timeout
  RUNNABLE --> TERMINATED: run() returns
```

sections.title: A thread moving through states
sections.content:
```java
Thread t = new Thread(() -> { /* task */ });   // NEW
System.out.println(t.getState());              // NEW
t.start();                                      // -> RUNNABLE
System.out.println(t.getState());              // RUNNABLE

// Inside the task, contention/wait move the state:
synchronized (lock) {                           // if lock held: BLOCKED
  lock.wait();                                  // -> WAITING (until notify)
}
Thread.sleep(500);                              // -> TIMED_WAITING (500ms)

// When run() returns -> TERMINATED
t.join();
System.out.println(t.getState());              // TERMINATED
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing BLOCKED (waiting for a lock) with WAITING (waiting for notify) — different causes.
Thinking RUNNABLE means 'currently running' — it means ready, running, or doing I/O.
Forgetting that sleep() puts a thread in TIMED_WAITING, not WAITING.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Six thread states: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
NEW→RUNNABLE via start(); RUNNABLE→BLOCKED via synchronized contention.
WAITING (no timeout) vs TIMED_WAITING (bounded) — entered via wait/sleep/join.
BLOCKED = waiting for a lock; WAITING = waiting for notify — don't confuse them.
RUNNABLE means ready/running/I/O, not strictly 'currently running'; run() returning → TERMINATED.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A Java thread is always in exactly one of six states defined by Thread dot State. NEW means the thread was created but start hasn't been called. RUNNABLE means start was called and the thread is ready, running, or doing I/O — the JVM combines ready and running under one label, so RUNNABLE doesn't strictly mean currently running. BLOCKED means the thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock to enter a synchronized region. WAITING means it's waiting indefinitely after calling wait, join, or park without a timeout. TIMED_WAITING means it's waiting for a bounded time after sleep, wait with a timeout, or join with a timeout. And TERMINATED means run has finished, normally or by exception. The transitions are: start moves NEW to RUNNABLE; synchronized contention moves RUNNABLE to BLOCKED and back to RUNNABLE when the lock is acquired; wait, sleep, or join move to WAITING or TIMED_WAITING and notify or a timeout returns to RUNNABLE; and run returning moves to TERMINATED. The common mistake is confusing BLOCKED, which is waiting for a lock, with WAITING, which is waiting for a notify.
